steps.title: Energy is stored
steps.body: Energy is not a substance you can see. It is a quantity that is **conserved**: in a closed system the total stays the same however the system changes, so if one store goes down another must go up. A moving bus has energy in its **kinetic** store. A book on a shelf has energy in its **gravitational potential** store because of where it is.

visuals.alt: A moving bus labelled kinetic store and a book on a high shelf labelled gravitational potential store

visuals.problem: A skateboarder rolls down a ramp, along the flat, and stops. Describe the energy stores and transfers.

steps.text: At the top: energy in the gravitational potential store of the skateboarder
Rolling down: energy is transferred mechanically to the kinetic store
Slowing on the flat: friction transfers energy to the thermal store of the wheels and the ground, and it dissipates to the surroundings. The total stays the same throughout.

check.prompt: A cyclist is freewheeling along a flat road at a steady speed. Which store holds the energy of their motion?
check.solution: An object that is moving has energy in its kinetic store.

steps.title: Kinetic energy: half m v squared
steps.body:
$$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$$

$E_k$ in joules, $m$ in kilograms, $v$ in metres per second. Square the speed before you multiply.

visuals.problem: A car of mass 1200 kg at 15 m/s

check.prompt: A 2 kg ball rolls at 3 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in joules.

steps.title: Double the speed, four times the energy
steps.body: Because the speed is squared, kinetic energy grows faster than speed. Drag the slider and watch the curve: at twice the speed the energy is four times as big, at three times the speed it is nine times.

visuals.fallback: A graph of kinetic energy against speed for a 2 kg object curves upward: 4 J at 2 m/s, 16 J at 4 m/s, 36 J at 6 m/s, 64 J at 8 m/s.

visuals.problem: A 1000 kg car speeds up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s. How many times bigger is its kinetic energy?

steps.note: three times the speed, nine times the energy
the mass cancels in a ratio, so you do not need it

check.prompt: The same 2 kg ball now rolls at 6 m/s, twice as fast. Calculate its kinetic energy in joules.
check.solution: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 36 = 36$ J, four times the 9 J at 3 m/s.

steps.title: Gravitational potential energy: m g h
steps.body:
$$E_p = m g h$$

$g$ is the gravitational field strength, $9.8$ N/kg on Earth. $h$ is the height **gained**, not the height above sea level.

visuals.problem: A 50 kg climber goes up 20 m

check.prompt: A 3 kg bag is lifted 2 m onto a table. Take $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained, in joules.

steps.title: Rearranging for speed
steps.body: Questions often give the energy and ask for the speed. Rearrange first, substitute second, square root last.

visuals.problem: A 2 kg object has 64 J of kinetic energy. Find its speed.

steps.title: Your turn: falling objects
steps.body: When something falls, energy moves from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store. If nothing is lost to the surroundings, $m g h = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$. Drag the ball to a height and see the speed it reaches.

visuals.fallback: Speed at the bottom rises with the square root of the height: 4.4 m/s from 1 m, 9.9 m/s from 5 m, 14 m/s from 10 m.

check.prompt: A ball is dropped from 5 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg, calculate its speed when it hits the ground, in m/s.

steps.title: Grade 9: why the mass cancels, and what happens when energy is lost
steps.body:
Set the two stores equal and the mass appears on both sides: $m g h = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ gives $v^2 = 2 g h$. So a feather and a hammer dropped in a vacuum land at the same speed.

In the real world some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the air. **Dissipated** means transferred to a store that is no longer useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings, which warm up very slightly. Questions give this as a percentage: if 20% is lost, only 80% of $m g h$ reaches the kinetic store. Multiply by 0.8 **before** finding the speed.

visuals.alt: Two bar charts: before the drop, one full bar for the gravitational potential store; after, a smaller kinetic bar and a thermal bar making up the difference

visuals.problem: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 5 m. 20% of the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the air. Find its speed at the ground. ($g = 9.8$ N/kg)

steps.text: $\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = 78.4$, so $v^2 = 78.4$ and $v = 8.9$ m/s. With no loss it would be $\sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 5} = 9.9$ m/s.

check.prompt: A 4 kg object falls 5 m and 10% of its energy is dissipated. Take $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Calculate its speed at the bottom, in m/s, to 2 significant figures.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$: square the speed first.
- $E_p = m g h$ with $g = 9.8$ N/kg and $h$ the height gained.
- Falling: $m g h = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, so $v^2 = 2 g h$ and mass cancels.
- Energy lost to the surroundings: scale $E_p$ by the percentage kept before finding $v$.

visuals.alt: A card showing the kinetic and gravitational potential energy equations with their units

questions.prompt: Which equation gives the kinetic energy of a moving object?
questions.solution: Kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$. Under AQA's normal rules you recall it, and you have to recognise it as the one you need: $mgh$ is gravitational potential energy and $mv$ is momentum.

questions.prompt: A ball of mass 0.5 kg moves at 4 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in joules.
A 10 kg box is lifted 2 m. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained, in joules.
A car of mass 900 kg travels at 20 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in joules.
A 30 kg child gains 2940 J of gravitational potential energy climbing a ladder. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the height climbed, in metres.
questions.solution: Rearrange $E_p = m g h$ to $h = \dfrac{E_p}{m g} = \dfrac{2940}{30 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{2940}{294} = 10$ m.

questions.prompt: A ball is dropped from a height, hits the ground, and bounces back up to a lower height. Describe the energy transfers, naming the stores involved, from the moment it is released to the top of the first bounce.

criteria.text: At release, energy is in the gravitational potential store
As it falls, energy is transferred to the kinetic store (mechanically, by the force of gravity doing work)
On impact, some energy is transferred to the elastic potential store of the ball and some to the thermal store of the ball and surroundings, and by sound
On the way up, kinetic energy is transferred back to the gravitational potential store, but less than at the start because some was dissipated, so the bounce is lower

questions.modelAnswer: At the top the energy is in the gravitational potential store. As the ball falls, gravity does work and energy is transferred to the kinetic store. When it hits the ground the ball squashes, transferring energy to its elastic potential store, and some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the ball and the ground and carried away by sound. As it springs back and rises, energy moves from the elastic and kinetic stores back to the gravitational potential store. Less energy reaches that store than at the start, so the ball does not return to its original height.
questions.solution: Name a store at each stage and say what transfers it. The word "dissipated" is what earns the last mark.

markScheme.description: Gravitational potential store at the start
Elastic potential and thermal stores at impact

questions.prompt: An object of mass 8 kg has 400 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed in m/s.
Put these steps in the correct order to find the speed of an object from its kinetic energy and mass.
questions.solution: Equation, rearrange, substitute, then square root. Taking the root before substituting is the common slip.

markScheme.description: All steps in the correct order

items: Take the square root to find $v$

questions.prompt: A diver of mass 60 kg steps off a 10 m platform. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg, calculate her speed as she reaches the water, in m/s.
questions.solution: All the gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy: $m g h = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, so $v^2 = 2 g h = 2 \times 9.8 \times 10 = 196$ and $v = 14$ m/s. The mass cancels.

questions.prompt: A cyclist and bike have a combined mass of 80 kg and travel at 36 km/h. Calculate their kinetic energy in joules.
questions.solution: Convert the speed: $36$ km/h $= \dfrac{36\,000}{3600} = 10$ m/s. Then $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 10^2 = 4000$ J.

questions.prompt: A roller coaster car of mass 500 kg drops through a vertical height of 30 m. 20% of the energy is dissipated to the surroundings. Taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg, calculate the speed of the car at the bottom of the drop, in m/s. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution: $E_p = 500 \times 9.8 \times 30 = 147\,000$ J. 80% is transferred to the kinetic store: $E_k = 117\,600$ J. Then $v^2 = \dfrac{2 \times 117\,600}{500} = 470.4$, so $v = 21.7$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A student says that a car travelling at twice the speed needs four times the braking distance. Use ideas about energy to explain whether the student is correct. Assume the braking force is the same in both cases.
questions.solution: Level-marked. A grade 9 answer links the two equations explicitly: the energy that must be removed and the work the brakes do per metre. Note the question says braking distance, not stopping distance: thinking distance grows in proportion to speed, not speed squared.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about kinetic energy, work done by the brakes, and braking distance, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of kinetic energy, work done by the brakes, and braking distance with some links between points
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of kinetic energy, work done by the brakes, and braking distance with every step linked and correct physics terms

criteria.text: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$
Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times larger
The brakes must transfer all of the kinetic energy away by doing work
Work done equals force times distance, $W = F d$
With the same force, four times the energy needs four times the distance
Conclusion: the student is correct, stated clearly

questions.modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, so it depends on the square of the speed. If the speed doubles, $v^2$ becomes four times larger and so does the kinetic energy. To stop, the brakes do work equal to the kinetic energy, and work done is force multiplied by distance. The braking force is the same, so four times the energy means four times the braking distance. The student is correct.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg mass is dropped and hits the ground at 7 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg, calculate the height it was dropped from, in metres.

A pendulum bob of mass 0.2 kg is pulled to one side so that it is 0.1 m above its lowest point, then released. Taking $g = 9.8$ N/kg and ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed at the lowest point, in m/s.
questions.solution: $v^2 = 2 g h = 2 \times 9.8 \times 0.1 = 1.96$, so $v = 1.4$ m/s. The mass is not needed.

examTechnique.body: Under AQA's normal rules $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $E_p = mgh$ are equations you must recall. For the 2025 to 2027 exams AQA gave a full sheet with every equation on it; whether that continues for 2028 had not been confirmed when this was written, so know them. Either way the marks are for choosing the right one and using it correctly. Write the equation, substitute with units, then calculate. Always give the unit with your answer. Use $g = 9.8$ N/kg unless the question says otherwise.
examinerErrors: Forgetting to square the speed, or squaring the whole of $\tfrac{1}{2} m v$.
Using the height above the ground when the question gives a height gained, or the other way round.
Substituting a speed in km/h without converting to m/s.
Finding the square root before substituting, or forgetting the root altogether.
Leaving the unit off, or giving the wrong one: joules for energy, metres per second for speed.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer sets the two stores equal in symbols before putting numbers in, cancels the mass, deals with any percentage lost before the square root, and quotes the final speed to the number of significant figures asked for.
